title: The cue changes the stage
summary: Let the producer operate the lighting designer's portfolio through the selected cue. The stage itself is the work sample.

layout.skeleton: Place the identity above a single wide illustrated stage, followed by a horizontal cue list and the selected technique. Keep the controls adjacent to the stage.
layout.focus: The physical boundary of a wash, side light or backlight cuts across one original stage set, changing the shape of the scene with each selection.
layout.desktop: Give the illustration most of the canvas. Align cue names and technique notes below it with the lit set edge.
layout.mobile: Put the title, stage, three visible named cue buttons and selected technique in reading order. Keep the stage compact and keep the buttons beside the result.
layout.rhythm: Use the width of the stage and generous side margins to set the scale. Let cue names and the technique carry the rest.

imagery.subject: One original stage silhouette reacts to the supplied amber, white and blue light cues. Use amber #E8AD54 and ice blue #91C2E8 for the corresponding light.
imagery.crop: Keep the stage, beam boundary and one reference object visible at both widths.
imagery.fallback: Use a static stage drawing with a different beam shape for each cue. Always show the selected technique in text.

motion.effect: Crossfade the two illumination states while the set and controls stay fixed.
motion.reduced: Replace the state immediately and keep focus on the cue.

action.instruction: Use named native buttons with a visible selected state, update the stage and announce the current technique.
action.label: Use the actual cue name

why: The first interaction demonstrates the actual craft and lets a producer compare techniques without finding a separate demo.

sources.observation: Driving the car demonstrates the creative developer's work while the visitor explores the portfolio. The site lists a map, respawn and multiple input methods.
The studio offers standard Work and Connect navigation alongside an optional themed command interface.

credit: Original stage composition inspired by Bruno Simon and ToyFight. Use only original artwork.

title: The river changes the town
summary: Build the story along one measurable cross-section. A selectable elevation changes the illustrated bank and the list of affected places.

layout.skeleton: Set a short headline above one illustrated river section. Set the height rail beside the bank and pair it with the effect list at the selected level.
layout.focus: One water line crosses real marked elevations and shows exactly which named places become unavailable.
layout.desktop: Run the section wide with level markers along the left edge and the current effects legible to its right.
layout.mobile: Show a compact section, named level controls and the current list of closures. Keep the controls and result adjacent and readable.
layout.rhythm: Let the heights set the spacing of the rail. Group the effect list by the active reading, preserving every supplied fact.

imagery.subject: Draw an original riverbank section with labels for the path, ferry and bridge supplied by the brief. Use slate #70848A for the bank and gold #E4B659 to mark closures alongside text.
imagery.crop: Keep every elevation marker and crossing visible. Simplify the illustration before removing labels.
imagery.fallback: Use three stacked levels with the selected elevation and cumulative effects next to each. Keep selection operable by keyboard.

motion.effect: Move only the water line to the new elevation and update the effects immediately.
motion.reduced: Jump to the selected elevation without any movement.

action.instruction: Use named native controls for the exact elevations, expose the selected level and list all closures at or below it in readable text.
action.label: Use each supplied level and its units

why: The water line makes the relationship between height and closures visible. The text and controls still let a visitor answer the question quickly.

sources.observation: The ascent orders the exhibits by real altitude. The Kármán line is one of the named markers.
Depth provides the organizing scale of an explorable ocean story.

credit: Original river cross-section inspired by Neal Agarwal's single-axis stories.
